paras: The attempted lynching of Rube Jones took place at Fayetteville, Georgia, in July 1888, when a body of armed men broke into the town jail to lynch Jones, an 18-year-old Black prisoner accused of assault with intent to rape. Jones, who was not chained, ran through the crowd at the jail entrance and escaped under pistol fire, reportedly wounded. An Atlanta wire carried the story of his escape to papers from Pennsylvania to Minnesota.

According to an Atlanta account printed in the Maysville Evening Bulletin, Jones was arrested the week before for entering the room of a young lady, who held him until help came. Rumors of a lynching the next day were quelled, and a committal trial was held. The same account said that "Testimony for the defense seems to have aroused the ire of some of the citizens."

On Tuesday night, July 17, armed men came to the jail and demanded the prisoner, and Sheriff J. W. Brown refused. The men fetched tools from a blacksmith shop, battered down the wooden outer door in a few minutes, passed an unlocked second door, and pounded the lock of the iron inner door until it could be pried off. The Savannah Morning News put the work on the doors at about an hour.

When four of the party entered, Jones, who was not in a cell, dashed past them and through the crowd at the entrance before it understood what had happened. Someone shouted "Shoot him!" and at least four pistol shots were fired as the crowd gave chase, and many thought he had been killed. Later that night A. E. Stokes, clerk of the court, found Jones on his porch; Jones had hidden under the house and told Stokes he had been shot in the head.

On Wednesday morning Jones was tracked two or three hundred yards from Stokes' house, but he was not found and was reported still at large. No report of his recapture or trial, or of arrests of any members of the mob, appears in the coverage.

The earliest report was a two-sentence Atlanta wire, dated July 19 in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, saying that Jones "resisted and escaped." A longer version adding that he was "not manacled" and "at large, but wounded" ran on July 20 under headlines such as "Escaped from the Lynchers" in the Rock Island Daily Argus and "Ran the Gauntlet of a Mob" in the St. Paul Daily Globe. Condensed-news columns in Waterbury, Connecticut, and Freehold, New Jersey, reduced it to a single sentence.

The fullest account, an Atlanta letter in the Maysville Evening Bulletin, was headlined "WOULD-BE LYNCHERS" but called Jones "the rapist" and "the criminal" although he had only been committed for trial. In Georgia, the Savannah Morning News gave the episode one unnamed paragraph in its state news column, calling the prisoner "the victim," and the Hillsboro Recorder in North Carolina reprinted that paragraph on July 26. None of these papers commented on the attack in an editorial.

The Atlanta letter and the Savannah column place the attack on Tuesday night, July 17, while wire versions dated July 19 say it happened "last night," which would be July 18. The letter's sequence of Tuesday-night shooting and Wednesday-morning search supports the earlier date. The wire described the charge as rape, while the fuller accounts called it attempted rape or assault with intent to rape.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Rube Jones
bases: An armed body of men battered down the Fayetteville jail doors to lynch a prisoner charged with rape, who escaped through the crowd under fire (A1, A2, A3).

A crowd of armed men, four of whom entered the jail, acted without authority against the sheriff's refusal to punish a prisoner accused of rape, but Jones escaped and was reported alive and at large, so no one was killed (A2, A3, A5).
An Atlanta wire (A1, A5), a fuller Atlanta letter (A2) and a Georgia news column (A3) agree that a mob broke into the jail to lynch Jones and that he escaped through the crowd.

accounts.label: Atlanta wire
accounts.gist: A mob broke open the jail doors expecting to lynch Jones, aged 18, held on a charge of rape; unmanacled, he dashed through the mob and was at large but wounded.

accounts.label: Atlanta letter (Maysville Evening Bulletin)
accounts.gist: Defense testimony at the committal trial angered citizens; armed men demanded Jones, the sheriff refused, the doors were battered with blacksmith's tools, and Jones ran through the crowd under fire and hid under the court clerk's house.

accounts.label: Georgia news column (Savannah Morning News)
accounts.gist: A desperate Tuesday-night effort to lynch an unnamed colored prisoner held for attempted rape; about an hour to batter down the doors before he escaped in the darkness.

framing.detail: The Maysville Evening Bulletin headlined 'WOULD-BE LYNCHERS' but called Jones 'the rapist' and 'the criminal' though he had only had a committal trial.
Northern and western dailies ran the short Atlanta wire under escape headlines such as 'Escaped from the Lynchers' and 'Ran the Gauntlet of a Mob'.
The Savannah Morning News carried an unnamed one-paragraph item in its Georgia column, calling Jones 'the victim'.
